runs.text: A social-impact website concept connecting women’s skills with real opportunities.
PROJECT DECK  •  WEBSITE DESIGN  •  BUSINESS MODEL
Her Skills. Her Income. Her Independence.
A simple digital bridge between women with skills and people looking for services.
Talented women may lack visibility, customer access, or a simple way to present their work.
A free-to-start directory where women can list skills, showcase work, and receive enquiries.
More visibility, new earning opportunities, and stronger local women-led businesses.
Make skills discoverable. Make opportunities easier to reach.
The project starts with a common challenge: skill alone does not guarantee access to customers.
Work is shared only within a small personal network.
New customers may not know who to contact or what to expect.
Some service providers may not have a website or online portfolio.
Customers search across social media, messages, and referrals.
Design principle: keep it simple, mobile-friendly, and easy to understand.
Add skills, service area, sample work, and contact preference.
Customers browse categories and find relevant profiles.
Customer sends an enquiry or contacts the provider.
Provider can add portfolio examples and request feedback.
MVP principle: begin with profiles and enquiries; add advanced features only after testing.
Design for two main groups, with a clear experience for each.
• Community members who want to support women-led work
A focused structure keeps the first version manageable.
Future pages: dashboard • booking requests • reviews • learning resources
The homepage should explain the value within the first few seconds.
Show categories, simple steps, and safety guidance.
Make it easy for customers to find a relevant service.
Name or display name, skill, sample work, and enquiry action.
Avoid pay-to-win ranking in the early version.
Each profile should be clear, respectful, and easy to contact.

Display name, skills, location area, description, portfolio, contact preference.

4. Agree on price and delivery directly
Important: the first version is a discovery and enquiry platform—not a payment processor or guarantee of service quality.
Trust is built through clarity, honest expectations, and a visible way to ask for help.
What the platform does—and does not do
How do I contact a provider?
How can I report a concern?
Copywriting rule: use simple language; do not promise guaranteed income, verified safety, or guaranteed customers.
How the website will be managed
A small admin workflow keeps listings useful and the platform safer.
Review categories, broken links, and feedback.
Track impact metrics and improve the experience.
A women-focused platform must put user control and responsible handling first.
Publish a profile only after the person agrees.
Collect only what the platform needs.
Use city or service area instead.
Offer a clear way to report scams or harmful listings.
Say exactly what has—and has not—been checked.
No harassment, discrimination, or misleading income claims.
For a real launch: publish a privacy notice and terms, set an admin access policy, and seek appropriate legal guidance.
Keep the student prototype free; test demand before adding monetisation.
Revenue is a hypothesis—not a guarantee. Validate willingness to pay and protect fair access before charging.
How to attract the first users
Start local, learn quickly, and build trust through community relationships.
Share the prototype with student groups and local community organisations.
Invite artisans, home bakers, tutors, and small business owners.
Post short skill spotlights with permission and clear calls to action.
Let providers invite another woman; reward with visibility, not money at first.
Pilot goal: learn whether people can find a relevant provider and successfully send an enquiry.

A small digital idea with the potential to create meaningful opportunities.
A diversified model can support the platform while keeping basic access affordable for women.
Optional paid visibility for providers who want extra promotion. Clearly label sponsored listings.
A small fee on confirmed bookings only, introduced after demand and fair pricing are tested.
Affordable add-ons such as portfolio templates, enquiry insights, or appointment tools.
Partner with NGOs, colleges, and skill programmes for workshops or sponsored learning.
Responsible sponsorships from relevant businesses, CSR initiatives, or community partners.
Optional help with photos, profile writing, catalogues, or digital storefront setup.
Profit formula: Revenue − operating costs = surplus/profit. Track hosting, support, moderation, marketing, and payment costs.
Start free, test willingness to pay, and never promise guaranteed income or customers.
Multilingual access can help women and customers use HerHunar in the language they know best.
A visible menu for English, Hindi, and regional languages based on user needs.
Let providers write bios and service details in their preferred language.
Use reviewed translations and clear labels; let users switch languages anytime.
Fast pages, readable text, and simple forms for slower connections and basic phones.
Readable contrast, keyboard support, consent controls, reporting, and privacy-first profiles.
Regional search terms and community partnerships can help more users discover services.
Rollout plan: launch with English + Hindi, then add regional languages in phases after user testing.
Goal: remove language barriers—not claim every language is already supported. Validate translations before launch.
